safe-paper-action.kind: original delivery protocol, not completed learner work
givenFacts: Provide four spoken picture cards: clean paper offcut left from class drawing; empty used plastic package; food peel; worn-out cloth. These are different human-produced waste materials, not actual garbage for handling.

Provide one actual clean non-confidential paper offcut with an unused side, a fresh sheet, and a classroom labelling job requiring only a small writable piece. Teacher confirms reuse is permitted and safe.
Child can reuse the offcut for the label rather than take a fresh sheet. Teacher records what actually happened; no fabricated waste weight or environmental saving is supplied.
safe-paper-action.question: Identify the waste material kinds. Plan how to avoid wasting the clean offcut, including permission and the job it will do. Actually carry out the reuse action and show the resulting label. Explain why using the otherwise discarded paper and avoiding a fresh sheet matters. Name an alternative action if the offcut contains private writing or is dirty; ask an adult for a safe suitable piece rather than reuse unsuitable material.
safe-paper-action.expectedEvidence: Different waste kinds identified; feasible stated plan; actual witnessed action/result; reason for each chosen action, not a poster-only response.
safe-paper-action.nearMiss: A named object, copied authored model, single-condition match or memorised fact omits the required independent comparison, performance or supported explanation. Do not award complete source-task evidence for it.
safe-paper-action.changedCase: An offcut now has private information or is wet/dirty: it is not supplied to the child; identify the safety/privacy condition and choose an adult-approved alternative.
safe-paper-action.attributionLimits: No child handles bins, broken glass, batteries, food waste or sharp/dirty materials. Actual enactment remains required at delivery; providing a plan does not establish that it occurred.

same-job-material-life.kind: original hypothetical comparison with stipulated programme conditions
givenFacts: Two intact classroom book-support frames A and B do the SAME job: keep the same small set of books upright on a shelf. Both are structures because their bases and upright supports carry the book load.

A is selected solid wood from trees: rigid, opaque; in this model a loose wooden support can be repaired by an adult. B is selected manufactured plastic made using fossil feedstocks: rigid, opaque; in this model a cracked support cannot be repaired by the class. No claim is made about every wood or plastic object.

Both are useful while safe and intact. Reusing an unneeded intact support with another class avoids discarding a usable object. For this model the school accepts clean uncoated paper/card for recycling but accepts neither damaged frame in its ordinary classroom recycling. These are explicit fictional programme conditions, not a real municipality rule.

A second same-purpose pair is a dry classroom storage tray made from selected card versus selected rigid reusable plastic. Model facts: both hold the same dry crayons; card tray softens if wet, plastic tray can be cleaned and reused. No absolute lifecycle winner or numerical impacts are supplied.

For observable-characteristic evidence provide actual clean safe uncoated paper/card, a smooth wooden block and an intact flexible plastic sheet, checked by the adult. Learner looks, touches and gently bends each; optional small water-drop demonstration is adult-supervised away from electricity. Record what the actual sample does; do not infer from generic material names. The comparison-frame properties above remain stipulated model facts, not claimed observations of a real product.
same-job-material-life.question: Compare the same-purpose frames by material, natural raw source, suitability, possible effect on people who use/repair them, and what happens when worn or no longer needed. Compare the tray pair for dry use and for a changed wet-use condition. Explain a choice using supplied properties and a tradeoff. Explain how reuse/repair can reduce discarded material, while new material extraction and discarded waste can affect the environment. Say what else you would need before claiming one frame always has lower total environmental impact. Observe the actual supplied samples and describe two properties for each in everyday words; distinguish the object from its material and use an observed property as a reason for a possible job. A supplied picture alone does not certify firsthand observation or the complete five-word/three-material topic repertoire.
same-job-material-life.expectedEvidence: Actual comparison of BOTH material-origin/end-of-use pathways for structures AND a second everyday object pair; reasoned people/environment judgment, conditional on facts. Actual direct observations of safe samples linked to uses; preserve complete contributor tests independently.
same-job-material-life.nearMiss: A named object, copied authored model, single-condition match or memorised fact omits the required independent comparison, performance or supported explanation. Do not award complete source-task evidence for it.
same-job-material-life.changedCase: The receiving class no longer needs a frame, or the local programme accepts a material it previously rejected: revise the end-of-use choice; material name alone is not permission to recycle.
same-job-material-life.attributionLimits: No natural-always-better conclusion; no invented carbon/durability figures; source facts support origins and reuse principles, while selected performance/repair/programme conditions are original stipulations.

load-support-and-fasteners.kind: original model facts and safe optional physical demonstration
givenFacts: Model chair C: seat supports a toy, four legs support the seat and toy, and crosspieces join legs into a frame. The floor supports the whole chair. A toy sticker on the seat decorates it but does not support the toy.

Model shelter S: two upright posts and a crossbar form a framework carrying a light card roof; the roof itself carries a few stipulated paper snowflakes. These are model loads, not a safe real-building design.

Fastener cards show: tape bridges two card edges; dried suitable craft glue bonds a flat paper label to card; a split pin passes through pre-punched card holes and holds a rotating pointer while allowing rotation; a staple through overlapping paper holds the sheets together. Each pictured joint and use is explicitly supplied.
Teacher may show intact safe models; no child must operate a stapler, sharp pin or tool to identify the fasteners.
load-support-and-fasteners.question: Identify the designed supporting structures and their loads, including an internal framework. Explain why the sticker is not a support. Explain how a chair leg supports the seat but is also part of the load on the floor. Change from chair to shelter frame without redefining all objects as structures. Create your OWN simple sketch or card model for this problem: keep a light toy above the table on a small stand. Show the supporting top and its framework/base, label the toy load, and explain how a chosen shape/structure supports it and connects to the real problem. A decoration or copied authored picture is insufficient. If a proposed stand lacks support, revise the sketch and explain the change. No quantitative force calculations or full construction-testing cycle is required. Identify each fastener and describe its appropriate supplied use. Choose a split pin for the pointer and explain why fixing the pointer flat with glue changes its movement.
load-support-and-fasteners.expectedEvidence: Recognises load-support relation and framework across both models; identifies at least the four supplied fastener kinds with uses; distinguishes joining from merely naming an object. For the ModelSketch contribution actually create and explain an own support solution; do not treat recognition of authored models alone as this procedural contribution.
load-support-and-fasteners.nearMiss: A named object, copied authored model, single-condition match or memorised fact omits the required independent comparison, performance or supported explanation. Do not award complete source-task evidence for it.
load-support-and-fasteners.changedCase: Glue the pointer flat or remove a supporting crossbar: predict which specified function changes and why, without claiming every real structure will collapse.
load-support-and-fasteners.attributionLimits: Authored recognition alone does not establish ModelSketch mastery: this bank separately requires the learner to create and explain an own support model for its contributor evidence, while complete other contributor repertoires remain separate.

material-fibre-origin.kind: original whole-claim age-fit witness and source-origin component assessment
givenFacts: Provide spoken picture/source cards: cotton fibre grows around cotton seeds; wool fibre comes from sheep fleece; silk comes from silkworm cocoon fibres; wood comes from trees; stone is collected from rock. These are natural material origins.

Provide selected manufactured-material cards: nylon and polyester are manufactured synthetic fibres; ordinary manufactured soda-lime glass uses sand plus other mineral ingredients; selected paper is made with wood fibres; selected conventional fossil-feedstock plastic is manufactured using oil- or gas-derived feedstock. These are examples, not universal claims about all plastics or glasses.

Four original clothing-label cards, spoken aloud: cotton; wool; polyester; nylon. No percentages, independent reading or polymer chemistry are learner gates. All garments are made by people, but their fibres have different origins.

A washed/spun/woven cotton shirt still contains natural cotton fibre: processing a natural fibre into cloth does not make that fibre synthetic. Manufactured glass and paper involve making a different material from natural starting material.

Changed-context model: bags B1 and B2 are otherwise similar sewn cloth shopping bags, both made by people in a factory. Spoken label B1 says cotton; spoken label B2 says polyester. These are declared original model facts, not a claim about an unlabelled real product.
material-fibre-origin.question: Sort the material and fibre cards and explain the natural-origin versus manufactured-material distinction, including wood/stone and glass/plastic as well as fibres. Sort all four spoken clothing labels into natural/synthetic fibre groups, explaining why the fact a shirt was sewn by people does not settle fibre origin. Trace selected paper to wood, ordinary manufactured glass to sand/minerals, and selected conventional plastic to fossil feedstock; identify that knowing one origin does not prove every material follows it. Transfer to washed woven cotton versus manufactured polyester: does washing/weaving turn cotton into a synthetic fibre? Explain.
material-fibre-origin.expectedEvidence: ALL THREE current Natural and made materials canonical criteria are represented by the whole-claim witness. D2.8 itself requires only the raw-source component plus use in structures; successful origin tracing alone must not award the whole fibre/label claim.
material-fibre-origin.nearMiss: A named object, copied authored model, single-condition match or memorised fact omits the required independent comparison, performance or supported explanation. Do not award complete source-task evidence for it.
material-fibre-origin.changedCase: For the two explicitly supplied factory-made bags B1 (cotton label) and B2 (polyester label), a friend says both fibres must be synthetic because people made both bags. Decide whether that follows and explain each fibre origin using the labels and source facts, rather than appearance or the object’s manufacture. Keep the selected conventional-plastic source example qualified; it does not establish that every plastic has the same raw source.
material-fibre-origin.attributionLimits: Positive age-fit review covers the complete unchanged three-criterion claim through concrete spoken labels and origin evidence; no independent reading, percentages or chemistry gate. Existing AU9–10 and IN3–8 scopes are preserved. The unrelated hard fair-test-design prerequisite is removed in this slice after independent-claim necessity review. Existing whole claim and all guides remain unchanged; source-origin success alone still does not award the complete textile/label claim.

dependencyDecision.reason: Natural/manufactured classification and raw-source tracing require identity and provenance knowledge; independently designing a controlled property/suitability test is not necessary. A thematic relation alone does not justify a hard or soft dependency.
independentWitnesses: A learner correctly sorts broad natural/manufactured examples and all four fibre labels, traces selected material origins and rejects woven-cotton becoming synthetic, while failing to control sample size/water/time in a separate waterproofing test. Target success does not require full fair-test mastery.

A learner independently controls a comparative test, records results and justifies a material use, while failing to identify natural/synthetic fibres or raw origins. Full testing mastery does not establish classification/provenance. These are hypothetical discriminating witnesses, not observed learner records.
dependencyDecision.preservation: The 4002 other edges remain exact, including both other soft consumers of Testing Materials for Uses and Natural and made materials’ two existing soft supports. No topic/guide/age/source scope is changed or retired. AU/IN independent fair-test duties remain represented by their unchanged associations and whole claims.
dependencyDecision.consumerReadiness: Removing an unjustified prerequisite can change future planner eligibility for this unchanged claim. It does not transfer mastery or authorize changes to stored learner estimates/history. No DB writes occur.
